episode_title: From Selling Tickets To Selling Experiences: Dan Rosenthal On Building High-Value Sales Teams

real_qa.q: What experiential hospitality experiences does Elevate offer at the U.S. Open tennis tournament?
real_qa.r: Elevate offers U.S. Open experiences that include arrival in an official US Open Cadillac with concierge guidance through crowds, access to exclusive hospitality space with premier food and beverage, front row baseline seating, in-seat service to avoid missing play, meet-and-greets with former players and champions, and the ability to play tennis with Andre Agassi and Arthur Ashe, plus trophy pictures. The in-seat service was created specifically because in tennis, walking the concourse or stairs distracts players, so drinks and food are brought directly to attendees.
real_qa.requete: US Open Elevate experiential hospitality experiences

real_qa.q: How does Elevate convince sports leagues and events to outsource hospitality and premium access instead of keeping it exclusive to sponsors?
real_qa.r: Dan Rosenthal explains that Elevate must convince rights holders on multiple fronts: first, that outsourcing creates incremental commercial value beyond standard tickets; second, that providing access to paying customers is beneficial rather than keeping it exclusive; and third, that fans will actually pay significant dollars above normal ticket prices for these curated experiences. The challenge involves aligning with operational teams to ensure seamless execution while remaining authentic to each specific event rather than repeating the same formula across different properties.
real_qa.requete: Elevate convince sports teams premium hospitality outsource

real_qa.q: What was Dan Rosenthal's early struggle in sales and how did he overcome it?
real_qa.r: Rosenthal was the worst salesperson initially but compensated by outworking everyone—being first in and last out, making more phone calls than anyone else. His breakthrough came when a senior colleague advised him to infuse his personality and understand rhythm like music, rather than reading scripts word for word. By understanding the beats and notes of a sales conversation, he was able to freestyle within the framework instead of following exact words, which transformed his sales performance into being one of the top sellers for four to five straight years.
real_qa.requete: Dan Rosenthal early sales struggles how overcome

real_qa.q: Why did the New York Yankees need to build an outbound sales culture when Dan Rosenthal joined in 2009?
real_qa.r: The Yankees had not had a full outbound sales culture or inside sales team before Rosenthal arrived. When the new stadium opened in 2009, the economy crashed, forcing the organization to change their business model. Rosenthal was brought in post-stadium opening to create an outbound B2B sales environment and build an entry-level sales team from scratch, as the organization had primarily relied on the brand value of winning baseball games rather than proactive revenue generation.
real_qa.requete: Yankees 2009 inside sales culture Dan Rosenthal

real_qa.q: How did Dan Rosenthal adjust his leadership and sales philosophy when moving from the Cleveland Cavaliers to the New York Yankees?
real_qa.r: Rosenthal initially tried to replicate the Cleveland playbook but quickly realized the Yankees culture was fundamentally different and required authenticity rather than copying. He had to recognize that the Yankees were primarily driven by winning baseball games, not revenue generation. Additionally, he learned that selling in New York operated at a different scale—deals had higher values, clients were more sophisticated power brokers, and presentations, polish, and business documents needed to be significantly elevated. He also discovered that hiring talent and leading people was far more complex than he anticipated and required multiple hiring cycles to develop competency.
real_qa.requete: Dan Rosenthal Cleveland Cavaliers Yankees leadership adjustment

guest.bio_context: Dan Rosenthal started his career in ticket sales with the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2004, where he became one of the top sellers for four to five consecutive years before moving into premium seating. He later joined the New York Yankees to build and manage an inside sales team, creating an outbound B2B sales culture from scratch. He currently leads Elevate's experiential hospitality group, partnering with major sports organizations and events globally to create curated hospitality experiences for fans.
